question: Why does keeping an open-ended multi-day work trial past 200 employees outperform standard technical interview loops?
guest: Normally when you are a small company, you have your first engineers contract with you instead of doing a LeetCode-style interview loop, because you are getting to the ground truth of whether you work well together. Usually companies stop doing that after a couple of hires, but we still have everyone hired on engineering and design spend two days in the office working on a freeform project. It is a frozen older version of the codebase with DevEx set up—just go do it. That serves three functions. First, it tests orthogonal things to standard coding interviews: can they go end-to-end in the codebase, are they agentic, and what do they build if left in a vacuum without a team, which reveals product sense. Second, it functions as a culture interview over four to six meals together. Third, it gives the candidate huge information about what day one actually feels like, leading to much higher fit on their end if they say yes.

The premise isn't established: there is no rigorous evidence that open-ended multi-day work trials outperform standard interview loops, at 200 employees or any other size. I'm answering from memory rather than a fresh search.

What supports the idea is that work-sample tests are among the better predictors of job performance in the selection research (Schmidt & Hunter 1998; Sackett et al. 2022). A trial also shows things interviews measure poorly, such as collaboration, communication, handling ambiguity and working in a real codebase. Companies such as Automattic and PostHog use paid trials well beyond 200 people and say they work well, but that is self-reported and not a controlled comparison.

The case against grows with scale. Sackett's re-analysis put structured interviews at roughly the same or better validity than work samples. Open-ended trials are hard to standardise, so evaluations become noisier and more bias-prone as more teams run them. They also cost considerable employee time, and they screen out candidates who can't take days off from a current job or caregiving, which narrows and skews the pool.

Trials can work if they are paid, structured and consistently scored, but "outperforms" is a claim, not a finding.

models.answer: Standard technical interview loops measure rehearsable proxies—isolated coding puzzles, abstract system design prompts, and polished behavioral stories—that correlate poorly with real execution, especially as candidates train specifically for rubrics and AI tools erode traditional screening signals. An open-ended, multi-day work trial replaces those proxies with ground truth: how someone navigates an unfamiliar codebase, scopes ambiguous problems, exercises product judgment, incorporates feedback, and ships real work alongside future teammates. Over multiple days, teams directly observe iteration speed, communication habits, and debugging instincts that brief interviews miss. Most companies abandon trials early to maximize recruiting throughput, yet past 200 employees, standardized loops invite interviewer calibration drift and compounding false positives that dilute talent density. Keeping the trial at scale acts as a deliberate forcing function that protects the hiring bar and culture—as companies like Cursor and Linear have demonstrated—while creating two-way conviction that helps close exceptional builders who want to experience the real team, problems, and pace firsthand.

Past 200 employees, day-to-day work shifts from greenfield building to navigating sprawling codebases, cross-team dependencies, and organizational ambiguity. An open-ended, multi-day work trial can outperform a standard technical interview loop because it samples the work the company is actually hiring someone to do. A candidate has time to clarify an ambiguous problem, decide what matters, make trade-offs, and revise their approach after feedback. The team can assess the result and the judgment behind it. A timed interview gives candidates fewer chances to show how they work through those decisions, and performance can depend heavily on familiarity with the format.

Past 200 employees, the trial also gives hiring teams concrete evidence they can compare using a shared rubric as more people get involved in hiring. Candidates get a firsthand look at how the team works, too. The extra time pays off when the task reflects the role, reviewers score it consistently, and the trial is paid and flexible enough for candidates to participate.
